subject: toucan
pitch: A keel-billed toucan showing off on a short mossy branch. A huge rainbow beak in lime green, sky blue and orange with a cherry-red tip, a glossy black body, a lemon-yellow bib, a ring of lime-green skin around each eye, bright blue feet and a scarlet patch under the tail. A single pink orchid blooms on the branch beside it.
reasoning:
I'm planning the toucan model's proportions and skeleton structure, thinking through real-world scale (around 50 cm body, 20 cm beak) and how to lay out the joint hierarchy starting from a root pelvis joint.

I'm working out the branch placement so the lowest point touches the ground plane, then sketching the bird's pose: body facing +Z, head and beak extending forward, tail curving back, with a spine chain running from hips through neck to head.

Now I'm defining the joint chains themselves — a spine chain with hips, chest, neck, and head joints, a tail chain curving backward and downward, and separate upper/lower beak joints for the jaw.

For the wings I'm keeping things simple, likely a slab or small sweep shape folded against the body rather than a fully articulated chain. The legs will follow a hip-to-ankle-to-foot chain, with the toucan's distinctive zygodactyl feet rendered in bright blue.

For the legs I'm placing hip, knee, and ankle joints down to the branch, using a thin blue-grey sweep, with toe spikes extending forward and back from the ankle to grip the perch. The branch itself will be a textured sweep along the x-axis with mossy green and brown mottling, anchored to a root joint that everything else hangs off of.

For the orchid beside the bird, I'm planning a stem rising from the branch with petals arranged in a ring around a central sphere, using extrude shapes for teardrop petals placed via ring-generated frames with appropriate direction vectors.

For coloring, I'm thinking glossy black for the body and a gradient beak that transitions from lime green at the base through sky blue and orange to a cherry-red tip, using a paint function keyed on z-position along the beak's surface coordinates.

The beak itself needs to be huge and bulbous — about 0.2m long, 0.1m deep at the base tapering to a narrow tip — so I'm planning to loft it from stations along its length, built as a child joint off the head.

For the lower jaw, I'll give it its own joint positioned at the back of the beak, bound to a separate lofted sweep so the upper and lower beak move independently. Both pieces can use the same rainbow paint function keyed on z-position, applying it as the loft's color option.

The jaw joint's rotation axis doesn't need precise derivation since I'll just apply a small pose rotation about x to crack the beak open slightly for visual flair, with the lower beak mesh rigidly following since it's a child of that joint. I'll skip over-engineering this and move on to the head, which should be black like a toucan's.

For the head I'm going to use a plain SphereGeometry scaled slightly to look egg-shaped, since mixing raw three.js primitives with the SDK is fine for simple parts. For the body I'm considering a loft along a spine chain so it deforms naturally with bending, skinned to the nearest joints along that path.

I'm sketching out a series of cross-section stations from hip to neck, each with a width and height, following the curve of the spine from the lower back up toward the head, to give the body its rounded, perched-bird silhouette.

For coloring, I'm planning to use a paint function keyed on position rather than separate meshes: black for most of the body, a yellow patch across the throat and chest, and red near the undertail area, all blended based on y/z coordinates on the single lofted body mesh.

For the head, I want a solid black base with a lime green ring around each eye, plus small spheres for the white eye and black pupil, positioned at the eye centers on the sphere geometry.

Since the head sphere geometry centers at the "at" position, I can place paint coordinates in world space directly for the eye rings. Now I'm working out the tail structure as a chain sweep tapering toward the tip, with a scarlet patch marking the undertail coverts.

Figuring out parenting logic here—I need a distinct root joint since the chain creation will auto-name its first joint, so I'm thinking of placing a separate "root" joint at the hip position and letting the spine chain attach to it via nearest-joint resolution, avoiding naming collisions.

I'll keep naming explicit by passing `parent: "root"` directly, then build the spine chain with named joints spine1, chest, neck, head, referencing them by string name afterward. Then I'm attaching a jaw joint parented to "head" positioned slightly below the head tip.

Now I'm working out the wings: placing shoulder and wrist joints along a chain, then lofting a flat wing shape that's thin along the x-axis (binormal) and tall along y (normal) to match a wing folded flat against the flank.

I'm checking the wing's x-position against the body's half-width so it sits flush against the surface, and deciding to model each wing as its own bone chain with the loft driven by that chain's path points.

Next I'm defining the right wing as a mirrored version of the left (negating x) and setting both to black, then moving on to legs: bright blue chains running from hip to knee to ankle, with the feet resting on the branch surface and toes modeled as rods pointing forward and backward for a zygodactyl grip.

I'm sweeping the branch as a bumpy polyline with varying radius, applying a bark grain texture along the x-axis and layering a mossy patch paint on the top-facing normals for a weathered look.

With the branch resting flat on the floor, I'm adding an orchid growing beside the bird: a slender stem curving up from the branch, with a pink flower built from five petals plus a lip shape. I'm sketching a petal-generating approach using teardrop-shaped point sets around a center, oriented to face the viewer.

Writing petal geometry code...

Adding moss mounds on the branch as scaled spheres, then moving to the beak's color banding — lime near the head transitioning through sky blue toward the tip, matching the keel-billed toucan's signature multicolor beak pattern.

Now I'm defining the eye paint on the head sphere, calculating distance from each eye socket to create a dark pupil surrounded by a lighter iris ring.

I'm also writing the plumage paint function for the body, marking off a yellow bib region on the chest and a scarlet undertail patch near the tail base, with the rest defaulting to dark plumage.

Now I'm figuring out the tail sweep: coloring it black with a scarlet sector covering the underside, and setting up the radius taper function so the tail narrows along its length. I'm also wiring up the beak lofts to be bound to the head bone, and double-checking how the sweep function resolves bone weighting for rigid attachment.

For the wings, I'm mirroring the loft stations across the x-axis for left and right sides with uniquely named joints, and confirming the leg sweeps inherit their own chain's joint weighting. Now I'm working out the leg path coordinates, placing the hip joint under the body and figuring out where the knee and ankle should sit relative to the body's bottom edge.

I'm now placing the toe geometry just above the branch surface, calculating four toe segments branching from the ankle in a zygodactyl pattern (forward and backward toes), carefully keeping each toe's radius and vertical position clear of the branch while staying visually grounded on it.

Checking that the feet grip naturally over the branch top while verifying body and head proportions line up with the spine and beak joints. I'm working through the toucan's oversized beak geometry and sketching a slight jaw-opening pose by rotating the lower jaw about the x-axis at its pivot joint.

Setting up the joint hierarchy next — root, spine chain, jaw, tail, and paired wing and leg joints — along with body, wing, and tail loft stations sized to match a stylized big-bird silhouette. I'm placing a mossy orchid stem and petals near the branch with a simple petal-generating helper, then defining paint functions for the beak's color bands, the head's eye rings, the body's bib pattern, and mossy bark texture using noise and grain effects.

Writing builder setup code...

Finishing the plumage paint function with scarlet underbelly markings and black elsewhere, then assembling a mirror helper for leg/wing symmetry. Now I'm writing the final complete code, bringing together the paint functions, body parts, and assembly into the exported model.
